faqs.a: A cubic Bézier curve is defined by four points: P0 and P3 are fixed at (0,0) and (1,1), while you control the two handles P1 (x1,y1) and P2 (x2,y2). The curve maps animation time (x-axis) to progress (y-axis): a steep section means fast motion, a flat section means slow motion. The SVG on this page draws that exact curve.
faqs.q: What does the curve actually represent?

faqs.a: x1 and x2 must stay between 0 and 1 because they represent points in time — you cannot go back in time or skip ahead. y1 and y2 can go outside 0–1: values above 1 overshoot past the target, and values below 0 dip backward first, which is how bounce and anticipation effects are made.
faqs.q: Why are x values limited to 0–1 but y values are not?

faqs.a: ease is cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1): it starts fast, slows through the middle, and eases into the end. ease-in-out is cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 0.58, 1): symmetric, slow at both ends and fastest in the middle. They feel different — ease is snappier at the start, ease-in-out is calmer and balanced.
faqs.q: What is the difference between ease and ease-in-out?

faqs.a: Use transition-timing-function or the timing keyword inside the transition/animation shorthand: transition: transform 300ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1). The same four numbers also work in @keyframes via animation-timing-function and in JavaScript with element.animate().

faqs.a: Yes, and it is a deliberate feature: y-values above 1 make the animation overshoot its target before settling back (springy), and values below 0 make it pull back first (anticipation). This is how you build playful, physical-feeling motion without JavaScript physics.

faqs.a: Never animate layout-triggering properties like width, height, top, or left — they force the browser to recalculate layout every frame. Animate transform (translate, scale, rotate) and opacity instead; they run on the GPU and stay smooth at 60fps on phones.

css-cubic-bezier-generator.formula:
cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)

P0 = (0, 0)            start — fixed
P1 = (x1, y1)          first control handle — you set this
P2 = (x2, y2)          second control handle — you set this
P3 = (1, 1)            end — fixed

Constraints: 0 ≤ x1, x2 ≤ 1   (time cannot go backward)
             y1, y2 free      (overshoot and anticipation allowed)

Keywords: linear = (0,0,1,1) · ease = (0.25,0.1,0.25,1)
          ease-in = (0.42,0,1,1) · ease-out = (0,0,0.58,1) · ease-in-out = (0.42,0,0.58,1)

keyFacts: cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) defines a custom easing curve for CSS transitions and animations.
The four numbers are the two control handles of a Bézier curve from (0,0) to (1,1).
The x-axis is time and the y-axis is progress: steep curve sections animate fast, flat sections animate slowly.
x1 and x2 must be between 0 and 1; y1 and y2 can exceed that range to create overshoot and bounce.
All five CSS easing keywords (linear, ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out) are just named cubic-bezier curves.
The same function works in the transition shorthand, animation-timing-function, and element.animate().
